paragraphs: §0 — Bab 2 §7 conclusion (recovered on p309)

[p309 top, completing the broken §7 of Bab 2]: …in essence (fī al-maʿnā). Then [§7, in the numbering of Bab 2]: We further say to them: If you say that the Creator is living by a Life and speaking by a Speech (ḥayy bi-ḥayāh wa-nāṭiq bi-nuṭq) — for Knowledge for them is identical with Speech — then tell us about His Life: is it pre-eternal (qadīma)? If they say "Yes," we say: Then you must hold that the Life is itself living and speaking, and that the Speech is itself living and speaking. If they say "Yes," we say: Then what objection do you have to the claim that each one of these three is itself three? — since the Father had to have a Son and a Spirit alongside Him because He is living and speaking, the same must apply to the Spirit. If they say "The Spirit is not living and not speaking, and likewise the Speech [is not living and not speaking]," we say to them: Then tell us about the Speech — do you say that it is an agent (fāʿil), a Maker (ṣāniʿ)? If they say "The Speech is neither agent nor Maker," we say: Then what objection… [the argument continues into Bab 3 §1 below, which functions as the closing sting].
§1 (Bab 3) — The closing sting: the same proof binds anyone who claims an eternal Word, "like Ibn Kullāb and others"

… that. Don't you see — if someone were to say "Whoever is not moving (mutaḥarrikan) is incapable," and required that "Whoever is not walking is incapable" — would there be any distinction between you and him? And this argument binds anyone who claims that God's Speech is pre-eternal with Him, like Ibn Kullāb and others.

: ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿīd b. Kullāb al-Qaṭṭān al-Baṣrī (d. ca. 240/854) was the foundational Sunni theologian of the kalām al-nafsī doctrine: God's Speech is an eternal attribute subsisting in His essence, distinct from the created sounds and letters in which it is conveyed (an attempt to defend the uncreated Qurʾān while sidestepping the Muʿtazilī objection that the eternal-Qurʾān doctrine implies a second pre-eternal alongside God). His position was later canonized in Ashʿarī orthodoxy. Q's move here is decisive for the polemical economy of Maqala III: he aligns Christian qidam al-kalima with Kullābī qidam al-Qurʾān and treats them as a single target. The Bahshamī origin of this very grouping is directly attested in SUK 5434-5442, in a section headed al-naṣārā wa-l-Kullābiyya ("the Christians and the Kullābīs"): innā aqraba mā yuḥmalu ʿalayhi kalām al-naṣārā huwa hādhā al-wajh, wa-ʿalā hādhā jaʿala shuyūkhunā raḥimahum Allāh hādhā al-waḍʿ wajhan min al-muḍāhāh bayna al-Kullābiyya wa-bayna al-qawm ("the closest construal one can put on the Christians' speech is this, and on this basis our masters [the Bahshamīs] — may God have mercy on them — made this position a ground for muḍāhāh [side-by-side comparison] between the Kullābīs and that group [the Christians]"). The section then preserves the celebrated Abū Mujālid–Ibn Kullāb anecdote: Abū Mujālid (a Muʿtazilī) met Ibn Kullāb and asked: "If a man calls you hu mardī in Persian and another calls you innahu rajul in Arabic, do they disagree in anything other than expression?" Ibn Kullāb said no. Abū Mujālid replied: "Such is your situation with the Christians — for they say He is one substance, three hypostases, meaning by them an eternal life and a speaker-with-eternal-speech; the only difference between you is in expression." (SUK 5437-5442.) Q's terse "this argument binds anyone who claims that God's Speech is pre-eternal with Him — like Ibn Kullāb and others" is the Karaite descendant of this Bahshamī side-by-side comparison. The same Bahshamī apparatus that Muʿtazilīs deployed against Ibn Kullāb's Sunni doctrine is now redirected by Q against Christian Christology — with the added advantage that it convicts the Sunni-traditionalist mainstream too. See [[qirqisani-maqala12-mughni|anchor_grid_M3]] B3 for the broader Mughnī Vol. 5 (anti-Christian) + Vol. 6.1 (khalq al-Qurʾān) cross-reference; the SUK passage above is the more directly accessible Bahshamī-source-text. See also [[glossary]] s.v. al-Kullābiyya.
§2 — First proof: the Torah is from God; God is its writer; hence it is His creation

If one of those who hold the pre-eternity of the Word should ask us: "Do you claim that the Book of God which is the Torah, and others, is from God?" — we say: Yes. If he says: "And why do you claim that?" — we say: Because He [the Torah itself] says this is the Torah of God, and says in the account of mention of the two tablets [Exod 32:16]: וְהַלֻּחֹת מַעֲשֵׂה אֱלֹהִים הֵמָּה וְהַמִּכְתָּב מִכְתַּב אֱלֹהִים הוּא ("and the tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God"). He thereby informs that it is the writing of God, and God therefore is the Writer (al-kātib), and the Torah is His book which He wrote unto His creation.

[p308] And the writer of a book is its agent and originator, and the book is other than the writer (al-kitāb ghayr al-kātib); and since it is other than Him and no one apart from Him produced it, it is established that He created and made it.

If he should say: "Why may it not be other than God yet not be the act of God nor His creation?" — we say to him: That is not admissible, for it cannot but be either pre-eternal with God or not pre-eternal. If it were admissible for it to be pre-eternal with God, it would be admissible for it to be a god, since there is no pre-eternal except God, mighty and exalted. And it would follow that there be uncountably many gods — for the Creator's speech is innumerable, and all of it [on this view] is pre-eternal; for the Christians said "Word and Spirit are pre-eternal with God," and by this they required that God be three. So likewise whoever posits a million things, or more, pre-eternal with God, requires uncountably many gods. But if it is not pre-eternal with God, then it is necessarily temporally-originated (muḥdath), made (mafʿūl), created (makhlūq) — and when that is so, since it has no agent, originator, or creator other than God, it is established that God created it.
§3 — Second proof: it is impossible that God be Speech, since the speech is other than the speaker

A further aspect: it is not permissible to say that God is Speech (kalām); whoever says so has become an unbeliever. The speech is other than the speaker (al-kalām ghayr al-mutakallim), and must necessarily be an act for the speaker. And what God has done, He has created, innovated (ibtadaʿahu), produced (anshaʾahu), and invented (ikhtaraʿahu). So it is established that God's speech and His books — which are the Torah and others — are created, innovated, invented.

Moreover, God's speech to Moses: if it were pre-eternal, then God would have been speaking to Moses from all eternity, and Moses would have been spoken-to by God from all eternity. Since this is absurd, it is established that God spoke to Moses after not having spoken to him — and so His speech to Moses must be temporally-originated (muḥdath), since it came-to-be after not having been; and its Originator (muḥdithuhu) is God, Lord of the worlds.
§4 — Third proof: speech is letters in sequence; a single eternal letter is incoherent

Furthermore, speech consists of letters following one another, and words following words. So the second letter must come after [p307] the first letter, and the second word after the first word; speech is only intelligible when it follows in sequence, and were a single letter pronounced [alone], its meaning would not be grasped. On these people's view, then, what must be pre-eternal is [only] one letter of the speech, while the rest of the letters and the speech are temporally-originated — because all the other letters and words are only required after the first letter. So it must be that the pre-eternal [element] is just an alif or a bāʾ, and the rest of the letters and the speech are temporally-originated — and this is a demolition (hadm) of their position. The books and speech of God are therefore necessarily temporally-originated.

Furthermore, it does not even follow that that one letter must be pre-eternal — for if every verse is temporally-originated, then every alif must be temporally-originated, and if every alif is temporally-originated, then every wāw must be temporally-originated, since the like of the temporally-originated cannot be pre-eternal.

: The argument is a clean kalāmī sortie: speech as a sequence of discrete phonemes is, by its very phenomenology of sequence, incompatible with pre-eternity. A pre-eternal thing has no "second" — yet a bāʾ presupposes the alif before it. This was the standard Muʿtazilī rebuttal of Ibn Kullāb's kalām al-nafsī (which tried to escape precisely this objection by positing an "inner speech" behind the sequential phonemes). Q does not engage that escape here, but addresses it next in §5. The Bahshamī parallel is in SUK 10651-10656 (in the khalq al-Qurʾān section): fa-law kāna [al-kalām] qadīman lammā jāza an yuʿdam, wa-maʿlūm annahu lā yumkinu wuqūʿuhu ʿalā ḥaddin yuʿādu bihi, illā idhā wujida ḥarf ʿinda ʿadam ḥarf; yubayyinu mā dhakarnāhu wa-yuwaḍḍiḥuhu, anna aḥadanā idhā qāla "al-ḥamdu li-llāh," fa-innahu lā budda min an yaqūma ḥāl wujūd al-lām al-hamza, wa-ḥāl wujūd al-ḥā al-lām, wa-ḥāl wujūd al-mīm wa-l-dāl al-lām wa-l-ḥā, ḥattā lā yaltabis al-ḥamd bi-l-madḥ, wa-l-madḥ bi-l-dimḥ — wa-maʿlūm anna mā hādhā sabīluhu lā yajūz an yakūn qadīman ("if [speech] were pre-eternal it would have to be incapable of passing away; and it is known that its occurrence-in-a-form-that-is-restorable is only possible when one letter comes-to-be at the passing-away of another; this becomes clear in our example: if one of us says al-ḥamdu li-llāh, the lām must come-to-be at the passing of the hamza, and the ḥāʾ at the passing of the lām… so as not to confuse ḥamd with madḥ and madḥ with dimḥ — and it is known that what is of this character cannot be pre-eternal"). Q's "alif before bāʾ" and SUK's "hamza before lām in al-ḥamdu li-llāh" are the identical argument with different phonetic examples.
§5 — Fourth proof: God's speech is heard, written, read — and what is such cannot be pre-eternal. Refuting Ibn Kullāb's "soundless, letterless speech."

And among the indications that God's speech and books are temporally-originated: that they are heard with the ears, written with the hands, read with the tongues — and whatever is such is temporally-originated, not pre-eternal. For if it were admissible that the pre-eternal be heard with the ears, it would be admissible that it be touched with the hands.

As for Ibn Kullāb — he claimed that God's speech is not heard, while he claimed alongside this that God is seen with the eyes. He was asked: "And why do you claim that?" He said: "Because it is a speech without sound and without letters; and what is not so is not heard." He was asked: "And what is your proof that God's speech is not in letters?" If he says: "Because I have found created speech [to be] assembled letters, so if it were admissible for God's speech to be letters, it would resemble the speech of other-than-Him; and if His speech resembled the speech of other-than-Him, it would resemble other-than-Him" — we say to him: "Then what objects you to the claim that His speech is assembled letters and yet does not resemble the speech of other-than-Him? — just as you said that His speech is a known attribute (ṣifa maʿlūma) that does not resemble the attribute of other-than-Him. There is no distinction."

And it is said to him: "If you claim that God's speech is not heard and is not in letters because it does not resemble the speech of other-than-Him, then what objects you to the claim that [p306] He, glorified be He, is not seen with the eyes — since He is neither jawhar nor accident? For if it is admissible for you that He be seen, although He is neither jawhar nor accident, then likewise it is for His speech to be heard with the ears, even if it does not resemble the speech of other-than-Him."

: Ibn Kullāb's kalām al-nafsī doctrine (the "inner speech" / Innerwort) held that God's eternal Speech is an attribute subsisting in His essence, distinct from the sounds and letters in which it is expressed but not constituted. The sounds and letters are created; the speech itself is eternal. Q's objection is double: (i) the doctrine collapses into the ṣifāt vs jawhar/ʿaraḍ problem — if God's speech is an eternal attribute that does not resemble created speech, then by parity God's vision (which Ibn Kullāb affirms) should be possible without God being a jawhar or accident, which Q has already shown leads to absurdity; and (ii) the move equates the two heresies — Sunni eternalism about the Qurʾān and Christian eternalism about the Logos rest on the same evasion ("it's an attribute, not a substance, so the usual objections don't apply").
§6 — Fifth proof: if "no god but the Torah" makes the Torah a god, so too does "the name is the named"

And among what indicates that God's book and His speech which is the Torah and the like are temporally-originated and created: were one to say "There is no god but the Torah," he would have made the Torah a god and creator — just as were one to say "There is no god but so-and-so," he would have made so-and-so a god and creator. So just as the unbelief (kufr) of one who said so is established, so too is the unbelief of one who took the Torah as a god. And since the Torah is not a god, and everything other than God is temporally-originated and created, it is established that the Torah is temporally-originated and created.
§7 — Sixth proof: God's name is created sound-and-letters; only His essence (dhāt) is uncreated. (Against "the name is the named.")

If a questioner of theirs should ask: "Tell me about His saying בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים ('In the beginning God created') [and] אֲנִי יְהוָה ('I am the Lord [your God]') — is [His saying] 'the Lord your God' created?" — it is said to him: If you mean by "I am the Lord your God" the Creator who is the Lord God, then God forbid that He be created; rather, He is pre-eternal (qadīm azalī), He has always been. But what is created — on our view — is His utterance and His name (qawluhu wa-ismuhu), which is enumerated letters (ḥurūf maʿdūda) heard with the ears and pronounced with the tongues. So our saying Elohim — we intend by it the essence (dhāt) of the Creator, exalted be His glory; and the two names [the spoken Elohim and the spoken "Lord"] are two heard utterances, temporally-originated, created. But they claim that the name is the named (al-ism huwa al-musammā), no other.

: The ism / musammā debate ("is the name the same as the named?") was a major fault line of 9th-10th century kalām, with the Muʿtazila and most Karaites holding the name to be distinct from the named (the position Q defends here) and the Sunni traditionalists (and notably the Ḥanbalīs) holding identity. The Christian qidam al-kalima doctrine is parasitic on a strong identity-thesis: if "Word" (kalima) is identical with the divine essence it names, then the eternity of God entails the eternity of the Word. Q rejects the identity-thesis on Muʿtazilī grounds and thereby short-circuits the Christological inference. The same move undercuts the eternal-Qurʾān doctrine of Ibn Kullāb. The full Bahshamī version of the polemic — with the identical "fire" example Q deploys in §8 below — is preserved in SUK 10505-10534 (under the heading shubah al-mukhālifīn fī qidam al-Qurʾān): the eternal-Qurʾān party argues that "the name and the named are one, so since the Qurʾān contains God's names, it must be pre-eternal as He is"; the Bahshamī reply is wa-jawābunā anna hādhihi jahāla minkum mufriṭa, li-anna al-ism wa-l-musammā law kāna wāḥidan la-kāna yajib idhā sammā aḥadukum baʿḍ al-najāsāt an yanjus famuhu, wa-idhā sammā baʿḍ al-ḥalāwāt an yaḥlū famuhu, wa-idhā sammā shayʾan min al-muḥriqāt an yaḥtariq famuhu — wa-laysa al-amr ka-dhālik; fa-mā kullu man qāla "nāran" aḥraqa famahu ("our answer: this is gross ignorance on your part — for if the name and the named were one, it would follow that when one of you names some impurity, his mouth would be defiled; when he names some sweetness, his mouth would sweeten; when he names some incendiary, his mouth would burn. But this is not so: not everyone who says 'fire' has his mouth burnt.") The "fire" example is verbatim Q's in §8. SUK then quotes the Arabic verse law kāna man qāla nāran aḥraqa famuhu / lammā tafawwaha bi-smi al-nāri makhlūqu ("had one who said 'fire' been burned by his mouth, no creature would have uttered the name of fire"). The verbatim transmission of the example confirms the same Bahshamī pool is feeding both Q and ʿAbd al-Jabbār. See also [[glossary]] s.v. al-ism / al-musammā.
§8 — Against "the name is the named": fire is not in our mouths

What invalidates their statement: we may say "fire," and the name of fire is in our mouths, yet fire is not in our mouths. So too we say "the heavens and the earth and the whole world," yet none of these is in our mouths. The names are in our mouths, not the named (al-musammayāt).

Furthermore, their statement that the name is the named requires them to abandon their own doctrine — for in the Torah are the names of the heavens, the earth, the donkeys, the swine, people, and others. If the names of these things are themselves [identical with the things named], and these names are neither temporally-originated nor created, then on their own statement the heaven and the earth and all that we have enumerated are neither temporally-originated nor created. [p305] But if they say: "The heavens, the earth, and everything you have mentioned is created, while their names in the Book of God are uncreated" — this is a refutation of their statement that the names are them. And if the names of things are other than the things named, then the names of God are other than Him.
If they claim that the names of [created] things are other than them, but the names of God are not other than Him, their statement is invalidated from more than one direction:
- (i) We may know God yet not know all His names in all the languages we do not know — so what we have known is other than what we have not known.

- (ii) Our saying אֱלֹהִים, אֲדֹנָי, אֶהְיֶה, al-Rabb, al-Ilāh — these are names of God, yet they are our acts (afʿālunā). Our act is other than our Lord and Creator; so whoever denies that the names of God are the act of the worshippers is committed to saying that no one ever mentioned God or named Him by His name [which is absurd].

: A neat Muʿtazilī parry: speech-acts are afʿāl al-ʿibād (acts of the worshippers, in the Bahshamī ontology); if the names of God are God, then the worshippers' speech-acts include God Himself, which is absurd. The argument depends on the Muʿtazilī commitment that humans create their own acts (against the Mujbira / Compulsionists of §9). Q is here aligned with the Bahshamī school and against the Sunni occasionalists.
§9 — Senses of "X from Y": only one applies to "speech from God"
If someone says: "If the Torah is the speech of God, how can what is from God be temporally-originated and created?" — it is said to him: A thing from a thing comes in several modes:

- (i) the part from the whole (al-baʿḍ min al-kull) — as one says "the hand is from the man," because it is part of him; and this is impermissible of God, since He is not divisible (ghayr mutabaʿʿiḍ) and not partitionable.

- (ii) it is said "the fruit is from the tree" — meaning that it was grown from it; and this too is impermissible of God, mighty and exalted, since He is not a substrate of anything, nor described by the attributes of bodies.
- (iii) it is said "the oil is from the sesame," "the [olive] oil is from the olive" — meaning that it was pressed out of it; and God is exalted far above this description.

- (iv) it is said "justice is from the just-one, the act is from the agent, truthfulness is from the truthful one" — meaning that He did that and originated it. So our saying "the speech is from God" means He acted it and originated it — and everyone who holds a religion says the like of this. For al-Mujbira [the Compulsionists] say "evil is from God, and unbelief," in the sense that He created and originated them; and similarly the People of Justice (ahl al-ʿadl) say "the good is from God" in this same sense.
And the reader should not be wearied by this chapter, even if it is somewhat long upon him — for it has branches which require exhaustive treatment.

: Q's interjection is a rare moment of authorial voice. The "branches" are the multiple genealogies of pre-eternity-talk in 4th/10th-century kalām — Christian kalima, Sunni Qurʾān, and the ṣifāt debate generally — each requiring its own treatment. The phrase ahl al-ʿadl ("people of justice") is the Muʿtazilī self-designation; al-Mujbira ("compulsionists") is the Muʿtazilī polemical label for the predestinarian Sunni mainstream. Q's even-handed listing of both positions (both say "X is from God" in sense iv) is methodologically Bahshamī — but the framework he is borrowing is itself a Muʿtazilī one.
§10 — God speaks without tongue and lips: parity with seeing without eyes and knowing without an organ

If someone says: "If He spoke and spoke to Moses, did He speak with a tongue and two lips? If you say so, [p304] you have described Him by the description of bodies; and if you say no, this contradicts what is understood of the being-of-speech" — we say: One who speaks with tongue and lips cannot address two persons in a single state, nor speak to two persons in a single time. But our Lord — mighty and exalted — is able to speak to many of creation in a single state, with differentiated speech: one speech does not distract Him from another, just as the agent among bodies cannot perform many acts in different places in a single state, and cannot write in the moment he is erasing, and cannot annihilate in the moment he is shaping. But God — mighty and exalted — governs the heavens in the moment He governs the earth, and is able to create the fruit in the moment He forms the embryo, and to cause one to die and another to live, while He is an agent without instrument or motion or implement — and exertion (al-taʿab) and weariness (al-naṣab) and displacement and locomotion are inapplicable to Him.

What-is-other-than-God, mighty and exalted, does not act except by motion and displacement and exertion and weariness. Likewise also: speech proceeds from Him without His speaking with tongue and lips and effort and motions — even if what-is-other-than-Him does not speak except in this manner — just as He sees things without the sense-organ of sight, and knows things without a sign or knowledge inhering in His heart (ʿilm yaḥull fī qalbihi), even if what-is-other-than-Him does not see except by the sense-organ of sight and does not know except by knowledge inhering in his heart. Likewise: what-is-other-than-God sees what is in front of him and does not see what is behind him, and if there is a screen between him and the seen, he does not see — and God is the contrary of that.

Likewise: what-is-other-than-God does not speak except with tongue and lips and instruments and uvulas and motions, and cannot produce a khāʾ except from the throat, nor a shīn except from the side of the mouth, nor a mīm except from the lips; and cannot combine two letters [simultaneously]; and cannot speak to two persons in a single state with two words. But our Lord — sublime be His praise — is able for all of that in a single state.

: Q here deploys the standard kalāmī "parity of acts" argument: if God knows without an organ of knowledge and sees without an organ of vision (both granted by all sides), then God speaks without an organ of speech (lips and tongue). The phonetic detail — khāʾ from the throat, shīn from the side of the mouth, mīm from the lips — is the standard makhārij al-ḥurūf (loci of articulation) catalogue of the Arabic grammarians; Q deploys it to highlight the contrast between embodied human speech and disembodied divine speech.
§11 — The burning bush: God's speech inheres in the ʿawsaj, not in God

Then we say further: that [p303] speech from God, mighty and exalted, is only done by Him in other than Himself — not in Himself. And so are all His acts. As for us: all our acts inhere in us. But God, mighty and exalted, His acts do not inhere in Him — since He is the Creator and is not described by the descriptions of the temporally-originated.

If someone says: "Do you not say that God spoke to Moses from the bramble bush (al-ʿawsaj)?" — we say: Yes. And our meaning in that is that He created a speech and established it (aqāmahu) in the bramble bush; and God is the Speaker, and the locus (mawḍiʿ) of the speech is the bramble bush — just as the Ten Commandments / the verses are God's speech, while their locus is the two tablets. The speech is God's, not the bush's, and not the tablets', even if it has inhered (ḥalla) in the tree and in the tablets.

If he says: "But the bush said 'I am God'" — we say: Yes, God is the One who said that, by what He originated of speech in the bush by His power — not because He inhered in the bush; just as He created the human in the womb of his mother without inhering in the womb, as Job (peace be upon him) said [Job 10:10]: הֲלֹא כֶּחָלָב תַּתִּיכֵנִי וְכַגְּבִנָּה [תַּקְפִּיאֵנִי] ("Did You not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese?") and what follows.

: The ʿawsaj (bramble) is the Arabic equivalent of the Hebrew sneh of Exod 3:2-4 (the burning bush). Q's argument is structurally important: divine speech can inhere in a place (ḥulūl — a technical term in kalām for the relation of an accident to its substrate) without God Himself inhering there. This protects divine transcendence and explains the locus-language of theophany without endorsing any incarnational or ḥulūlī (Sufi-incarnational, applied later to certain mystical doctrines) reading. The same logic dismantles the Christian Incarnation: God's kalima could inhere in Jesus's body without God being in Jesus. The Bahshamī parallel is exact: SUK 10491-10497 has fa-in qīla: kayfa yakūnu al-qadīm taʿālā mutakalliman bi-kalāmin yūjadu fī ghayrih? qulnā: kamā yakūnu munʿiman bi-niʿmatin tūjadu fī ghayrih, wa-rāziqan bi-rizqin yūjadu fī ghayrih, wa-hādhā li-anna al-mutakallim huwa fāʿil al-kalām, wa-laysa min sharṭ al-fāʿil an [yaqūma] ʿalayhi fiʿluhu lā maḥāla ("if it be asked: how can the pre-eternal be a speaker by speech that exists in another? we reply: as He is a benefactor by a benefit that exists in another, and a provisioner by a provision that exists in another; and this is because the speaker is the agent of the speech, and it is not a condition of the agent that his act inhere in him inevitably"). The argument-structure is verbatim Q's burning-bush argument — God can be mutakallim by speech existing in the bush (= Q's kalām maʿṣūmun li-l-bush bi-fiʿl Allāh), just as He is munʿim and rāziq by acts existing in other beings. Q B3 §11's added biblical citation (Job 10:10, halōʾ ke-ḥālāv tatīkēnī… — God forming the embryo in the womb without inhering in the womb) is Q's Karaite scripture-anchor for what is, in SUK, a purely conceptual Bahshamī demonstration. See [[glossary]] s.v. ḥulūl / fiʿl.
§12 — Why doesn't motion-inhering-in-bush make the bush a mover-by-itself? Because speech requires agency, intention, and capacity in the speaker

One of them asked on this point and said: "If you claim that speech from God, mighty and exalted, has inhered in something, then that something does not become a speaker by it — so likewise it should not be admissible that motion, color, and composition inhere in something and that something not become a mover, colored, composed." — It is said to him: The distinction here is that the speaker is only a speaker by being the agent of the speech, willing it, capable of it, intending it (qāṣid ilayhi). And since the bramble bush in which the speech inhered is not intending, not willing, not an agent, it was not a speaker by the speech which inhered in it. And God — mighty and exalted — being the agent of the speech, is the One who speaks by the very speech that inhered in the bramble bush.
§13 — A further distinction: the bush can move and change color naturally but cannot speak unless spoken-through

Another thing: the bramble-bush tree may move and change color and be composed [in particular configurations], but does not speak such that it [genuinely] speaks, and is not addressed such that it speaks back. Do you not see that if someone addressed it intending to speak with it — it does not speak [back]; for the speaker [God] is the one speaking through it. But if a mover were to move it, or a colorer color it, or a composer [p302] compose it into a particular configuration, the bush would not resist that. So it is established that the bush is itself moving by the very [motion] that inhered in it [naturally], whereas the speaker by the speech that inhered in the bush is other than the bush, namely the One who is the agent of it.

Likewise: a person may write upon [the bush, e.g., on a wooden tablet] writing, yet the bush is not the writer, even if the writing has inhered in it — and so too the bush is not a speaker by the speech which inhered in it, because the meaning of "writing" and "speech" is the meaning of act (fiʿl) — and the bush is not an agent.
§14 — Why doesn't the parity-argument bind us? Because moving/colored/dead are by inherence, but speaking is by agency

If he says: "And if you claim that God, mighty and exalted, originates speech in other-than-Him so that He becomes thereby a speaker, then why is it not admissible that He originate motion, color, and death in other-than-Him so that He becomes thereby moving, colored, dead?" — we say: This does not bind us; rather, it binds you. For a thing is not dead because it produces death, nor moving and colored because it produces motion and color. If it were dead on account of producing death or colored on account of producing color, it would be impossible that anything move, take on color, or die which does not [itself actively] produce motion, color, and death. But since we observe many things that move, take on color, and die without being the agents of any of that, we know that a thing is not moving, colored, or dead by having done that — rather, it is moving, dead, colored by the inhering of death, color, and motion in it. But the speaker is only a speaker — an addresser (mukhāṭib) — by doing the speech and the addressing. And everyone who does so is a speaker.

: This is the crux: the kalām of ḥulūl al-aʿrāḍ (the inherence of accidents in their substrates) versus fiʿl (agency / production) gives Q a sharp distinction. Motion/color/death predicate of a body by inherence; speaking/writing predicate by agency. The Christian objection — "If God can be a speaker by producing speech-in-the-bush, He could be dead by producing death-in-the-bush" — collapses on the agency/inherence distinction. This is the technical apparatus that licenses Q's non-incarnational reading of theophany.
§15 — The reverse-direction objection: but God did create writing on the tablets and was thereby a writer…

Then the question was turned around on him, and it was said: "Has not God, mighty and exalted, created writing on the two tablets, and was thereby a writer (kātiban) — and created a sound, and was thereby a sound-maker (muṣwitan)? So what prevents that He create death and become dead-thereby, as He created sound and became sound-maker thereby? And so too let Him create color and become colored thereby, as He created justice and became just thereby — and likewise for motion." If he says: "It does not follow that by creating death He becomes dead, and by creating color colored, …"

- The polemical pivot from Christology to Sunni Qurʾān-theology (§1). The bab's opening sentence — "this argument binds anyone who claims that God's Speech is pre-eternal with Him, like Ibn Kullāb and others" — is the architectural keystone of Maqala III. Q is no longer arguing only against the Christians (as in Bab 2); he is generalizing to a class of qidam al-kalima positions which includes the dominant Sunni position. The cost is real: by adopting the Bahshamī apparatus he aligns with Muʿtazilī and against Sunni traditionalist theology. The pay-off is that he can run a single demonstration against Christianity and Sunni kalām al-nafsī simultaneously — which is the central economy of the bab.

- Five proofs that the Word/speech is created: 1. §2 (Exod 32:16) — the Torah testifies that it is "the writing of God," hence God is its writer, hence it is a created act distinct from Him; the only alternative is co-eternity, which proliferates uncountably many gods. 2. §3 — God cannot be speech; speech must be an act of a speaker, and what God acts He created. 3. §3 — were God's speech to Moses pre-eternal, God would have been speaking to Moses from all eternity, which is absurd. 4. §4 — speech is sequenced phonemes; the second letter presupposes the first; pre-eternity has no "second"; therefore at most one phoneme could be eternal, which is incoherent. 5. §5 — speech is heard and written and read; what is heard/written/read is created; therefore God's speech is created.

- The Ibn Kullāb engagement (§5) is the most explicit non-Christian polemical target in the bab. Ibn Kullāb tried to escape proof (4) and (5) by positing kalām al-nafsī — an "inner speech" that is neither sounds nor letters, eternal as a divine attribute. Q's reply runs the ṣifāt problem: if God's speech is an attribute that does not resemble created speech, then by parity, the visio Dei (which Ibn Kullāb also affirms) should be possible without God being a jawhar or accident — which Q has already shown to be absurd. So Ibn Kullāb's evasion fails on its own terms.

- The ism / musammā debate (§§7-8) is the cleanest example in Bab 3 of Q borrowing a Muʿtazilī commitment in the service of an anti-Christian (and anti-Sunni) argument. The identity-thesis ("the name is the named") was Sunni and Ḥanbalī orthodoxy; the distinction-thesis ("the name is other than the named") was Muʿtazilī and (Q makes clear) Karaite. The Christian eternal-Logos doctrine, like the Sunni eternal-Qurʾān doctrine, requires the identity-thesis to ground the eternity of the kalima in the eternity of God. Reject the identity-thesis and both doctrines fall.

- The burning-bush argument (§§11-14) is the bab's most distinctive philosophical-theological move, and the one with the longest legacy. The framework: ḥulūl (inherence of an accident in a substrate) versus fiʿl (agency / production). God's speech can inhere in the bramble bush as in the tablets — without God Himself inhering. The bush is not a speaker because speech is by agency, not by inherence; the bush is a mover because motion is by inherence, not agency. This protects divine transcendence while accounting for the locus-language of biblical theophany. The same logic — accident-without-substrate-of-deity — implicitly dismantles the Christian Incarnation; the kalima could inhere in Jesus's body without God being in Jesus, parallel to the inherence in the bramble bush.

- The fiʿl-vs-ḥulūl distinction (§14) is the bab's most technical kalāmī load-bearing wall. The objection "if God can be speaker-by-producing-speech-elsewhere, He can be dead-by-producing-death-elsewhere" is killed by the observation that motion/color/death are inherence-predicates (predicating of a substrate by inhering in it) while speaking/writing are agency-predicates (predicating of the agent by being his act). The bush moves because motion inheres in it; the bush does not speak because speaking is by agency, not inherence. The argument is recognizably Bahshamī — Abū Hāshim al-Jubbāʾī's aḥwāl framework lurks behind it — but Q deploys it with characteristic clarity.

- The §15 reversal is the natural countermove: "If God-creates-writing-on-tablets-and-is-thereby-writer, why not God-creates-death-and-is-thereby-dead?" — and Q's reply (cut off at the page boundary) presumably reinforces §14: writing is agency; death is inherence; the parity does not hold. The argument continues into Bab 4.
